I re-derived the SoA/AoS byte math (16 fields x 4 bytes = 64-byte Particle; 2,000,000 x 64 B = 128 MB vs 2,000,000 x 4 arrays x 4 B = 32 MB) and the stride-16 reasoning (64-byte line / 4-byte int = 16) myself and both check out. I read every sibling section this article links to (processes-and-threads.md 'What a context switch costs', virtual-memory.md 'Why is there a TLB, and what does a miss cost?', concurrency-race-conditions-locks.md '`counter++` is three steps, not one', space-complexity.md 'What an object actually costs: struct vs class in an array', arrays-and-dynamic-arrays.md 'Why the column-first loop falls off a cliff') and each genuinely supports what this article says it does, not just a resolving anchor. Design round 1's two findings are also visibly fixed: Figure 3 (array-of-structs vs struct-of-arrays box diagram) now exists, and both the ladder and false-sharing sections now open their results paragraph with a bolded lead-in phrase. Freshly comparing against two pages that currently rank for this territory: abhik.ai's 'CPU Cache Lines' guide states a generic 32-64KB/256KB-1MB/8-64MB table rather than measuring a real machine, has no quantified false-sharing benchmark, and only briefly gestures at AoS/SoA with a link out; diveintosystems.org's cache-coherence chapter has real numbers for exactly one effect (false sharing, via a sort-merge microbenchmark) and covers neither a latency ladder across cache levels nor AoS/SoA at all. This article does all four (measured sizes, latency ladder, cache-line-granularity stride demo, false sharing, AoS vs SoA), with every number either read live from the machine or produced by code the reader can run, and its citations, once corrected, hold up against the primary sources on inspection -- that combination is what pushes it clearly past both comparison pages rather than merely matching them.

issues.location: 'Two threads, two counters, one cache line' section, the parenthetical "four 8-byte counters fit in a single 64-byte line"
issues.problem: States as fact that the four `long` counters in `new long[4]` (32 bytes of data) fit inside one 64-byte line. That is true of the data's *size* but not guaranteed by its *alignment*: .NET only guarantees array data starts on an 8-byte boundary on a 64-bit runtime, not a 64-byte (cache-line) boundary, so depending on where the GC happens to place this particular array, the 32-byte block can in principle straddle two adjacent lines (e.g. bytes 48-79) rather than sitting inside one. It does not invalidate the measurement -- with 4 elements in 32 bytes, at least two of them are still forced to share a line by pigeonhole even in the worst-case placement, so false sharing still occurs and the reported slowdown is real -- but the sentence overstates certainty about something the program never actually checks or controls.
issues.fixLooksLike: Soften to something like "four 8-byte counters comfortably fit within one 64-byte line's worth of data" or add a half-clause noting the array isn't pinned to a cache-line boundary, so the claim matches what the code actually guarantees (the size relationship) rather than implying a placement guarantee it doesn't make.
